title: TB0-00383
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, (the claimant) a citizen of Colombia, claims to be in need of refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant is a 30-year old man from Bogota, Colombia. He had left Colombia to study in the U.S.A. on XXXXX, 2000 before his father, brother XXXXX, and 2 cousins had problems with members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC, guerrillas) in Bogota, which started in XXXXX 2000. He said the FARC were opposed to his relatives' involvement with XXXXX XXXXX, a community group that was assisting in the campaign of a candidate for Bogota Council. The FARC had demanded they stop their political work and, on at least 3 occasions in XXXXX, FARC men had confronted, threatened and attacked his relatives while they were putting up posters and canvassing people on the upcoming election. He said that in XXXXX 2000, his father received a phone call from a FARC member accusing his brother and 2 cousins of being members of the AUC (United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia, paramilitaries), who are enemies of the FARC. He said his father was considered to be a military target (death sentence), as well. In XXXXX 2000, someone fired several shots at his brother while living at their father's house after returning from Cali. The brother was injured but ran upstairs and saw through the window the shooters, who he believed to be guerrillas, flee in a car and a motorcycle. On XXXXX, 2000, his parents, brother XXXXX, sister XXXXX and brother XXXXX joined the claimant in the U.S.A. In 2001, he said they heard that the 2 cousins XXXXX and XXXXX had been "tortured and murdered" on XXXXX by the FARC in XXXXX, Valle, Colombia.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection for the reason that the panel does not find the material aspects of his story to be credible and/or his fear to be well founded. Alternatively, the panel finds that the claimant has a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Bogota. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity has been established by certified copies of his Colombian passport and other identification documents as tendered into evidence.2 Nexus
As the panel does not believe the claimant to have been or is targeted by the FARC, the panel does not see any connection to a Convention ground. Credibility

The determinative issue in this case is credibility and, in relation to that, the well-foundedness of the claimant's fear. The panel finds the claimant's story not to be wholly credible in its material aspects due to the following reasons.

During questioning by the panel to establish his fear and the facts of his story, the panel noted that the claimant had at least 25 times answered that he did not know, or could not recall, or was not sure about the facts, or with a "maybe." The questions included, among others, the nature of his brother's political activities, if his brother was able to confirm that 2 people looking for him were members of the FARC, if his brother reported the FARC men to police, why the FARC were interested in his cousins, what part of Bogota was his brother in when he was hit on the head and how many people attacked him, how his father knew it was the FARC who attacked the brother, when his brother had been shot at their house, why the father was sure it was the FARC who shot his brother, how many people were involved in the political movement, if the leader or other members of the political movement were attacked by the FARC, if his father had any evidence of his problem with the FARC, if other of his relatives still in Bogota have been confronted by the FARC looking for him, if they have not why not and why his brother and father are still targets of the FARC today since they had complied with the FARC demand to stop their political activities. From his answers, the panel drew a very strong impression that the claimant was not sure of whether or not the incidents that happened to his relatives were true or that he was really a target of the FARC. The panel consequently takes a serious negative inference in this observation and, therefore, does not believe that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant was or is a target of the FARC.

The panel notes that his Personal Information Form narrative (PIF),3 paragraph 1, identifies the candidate of the Grupo MIRA with which his family members were involved, as a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, but when asked about the candidate's name during his oral testimony the claimant avoided a direct answer and only said that the person directing the group was a XXXXX XXXXX, who was not mentioned at all in the narrative. The panel, therefore, takes a negative inference from this further indication of his poor understanding of his story, the basis for his claim and finding, on a balance of probabilities, that he was not or is not a target of the FARC as his fear was or is not well-founded.

Furthermore, the claimant still has close family relatives in Bogota. He said he has some "uncles or aunts that live in Bogota," and admits that he does not know if they had been confronted by the FARC looking for him. Furthermore, as to his story that his brother had been attacked, he had admitted during his oral testimony that Bogota is a high crime area, which indicates the possibility that if the attacks on the brother were true, they could have been perpetrated by common criminals in Bogota rather than the FARC. As to the killing of the 2 cousins, he had admitted he was not certain as to the identity of the killers or as to the connection of their killing with him as there was no conclusive determination of the identity of the killers by any government authority and as to why this event had any impact on him. This again casts a serious doubt on the FARC as being the perpetrators and eventually as to the connection of these incidents with the claimant personally. Based on these, the panel, therefore, does not believe that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant was or is a target of the FARC.

Furthermore, the panel notes that based on his testimony, his father and brother had effectively complied with the FARC demand to cease their political activities with the Grupo MIRA. Since this is the case, the panel believes that, even if his assertion that the FARC was or had been after him were true, which the panel does not believe to be the case, the FARC would no longer be after his father and brother and by extension, him.

Furthermore, it has been 10 years since he left Colombia in 2000 and since the incidents he alleges gave rise to his fear. Aside from his not having been seen personally by the alleged FARC members who threatened his relatives or who attacked his brother and cousins, there are changes to his physical appearance caused by aging which alter a person's recognizability. The panel also notes that the FARC has had compelling changes in its personnel, leadership and territories they had control of4 (discussed further under Internal Flight Alternative). Based on these time considerations, changes and other points, the panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that even if he had been identified and targeted previously, which the panel does not believe to be the case, the people who he said had targeted him as a member of his father's family would more than likely be no longer in the area they operated in or may not even be alive today so that they, effectively, would not know or recognize him if he, a member of a targeted family, were to return to Colombia today.

Furthermore, he did not tender into evidence any police report as neither his father nor his brother had reported any of their problems to police, any death note (sufragio) from the FARC that his father or brother may have received from the FARC, any evidence of his brother's injuries from the FARC as he said his brother never went to a hospital for treatment. He did not produce any direct supporting document of the threats and attacks he said were perpetrated on his father or brother. There is no conclusive evidence that his cousins were killed by the FARC or any connection of this incident with him personally. The panel draws a serious negative inference from the lack of any crucial documentary evidence in support of his claim. The panel notes that Maldonado5 proposes that the applicant's testimony will be presumed true unless there is reason to doubt it, which in this case there is as discussed in this section. The panel is of the view that Ahortor6 may be set aside, as well. In Osman and Taha,7 it was found that one could distinguish Maldonado and Ahortor in cases where the applicant could not reasonably explain an omission to provide material documentary evidence to corroborate her testimony. As the onus fell to the applicant in that case to prove her claim and she did not provide the necessary documentary evidence in support of it, the panel drew an adverse inference from this deficiency. In our case, the lack of this crucial documentation leads the panel to disbelieve, on a balance of probabilities, that the FARC is after him.

Based on the foregoing, the panel does not find a ring of truth on the overall credibility of the claimant's assertions that the FARC is after him and further, finds his fear not to be well- founded. Credibility - Subjective Fear

The claimant lived in the U.S.A. for 10 years from the year 2000, but did not claim asylum after he learned of his probable targeting by the FARC from his father and brother, who came to the U.S.A. in that year. He (or his family) did not take any prompt action at pursuing an asylum claim in the U.S.A. He said that his family claimed too late and was denied by the U.S. government.

The panel finds his inaction or lack of action of not applying for refugee protection soon after arrival in the U.S.A., and learning of his possible inclusion in FARC targeting of his family troubling, in that if he were truly in fear of being returned to Colombia, it would have been reasonable to expect that he would have taken steps and actions that reflect the urgency of his situation, that is, to apply for refugee protection as early as possible - in the U.S.A. If he did not succeed in the U.S.A. then he would have this further chance with Canada.

Professor Hathaway has said that it is appropriate to inquire into the circumstances of any protracted postponement of or inaction on a refugee claim as a means of evaluating the sincerity of the claimant's need for protection.8

In Leon, the claimant waited over five years to make a claim. Justice Muldoon of the Federal Court commented: It is incredible that he [the claimant] would believe that he could not make a refugee claim because he was an illegal.... That is incredible. That he would wait for five years in that belief, if that belief were true, is even more incredible.9

In the case of Juzbasevs,10 the applicant spent about four months in the U.S.A. without making a claim for protection, as she said she was advised by a relative that her case would not qualify. It was not considered to be reasonable that she would not have taken steps to seek proper advice on making a claim. In Gonzalez,11 the applicant and her sons lived in the U.S.A. for four years and three months without making a claim for asylum. A delay of four years was said to suggest a lack of subjective fear and it was open to the Board to reject the applicant's explanations. The lack of evidence going to the subjective element of the claim was found to be, in itself, sufficient for the claim to fail.

The panel, therefore, finds in this case neither a credible objective basis to the claimant's fear nor does it believe the existence of his subjective fear. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) - Another Part of Bogota

An alternative issue to the foregoing is internal flight alternative. The panel finds that the claimant can settle today in another part of Bogota, from where he used to live, the country's capital, even if the claimant's assertion that the FARC is after him were true, which the panel does not believe to be the case.

Taking into account the fact that the entire country has 45 million people, and Bogota alone has a mass of 8 million people, and the material changes to personnel and loss of its key leaders, the panel does not find it believable that the FARC still has the capability today to track him down, if the claimant were to settle in another part of Bogota.

As to state protection, the panel notes the following points from the National Documentation Package,12 as follows: * Colombia is a constitutional democracy. * Recent elections were generally considered fair and free and took place in an atmosphere of freedom, transparency and normalcy. * Civilian authorities generally maintained control of multi-level security forces consisting of local, national police forces and a national army.13 * The National Police are responsible for internal law enforcement, shared with the Department of Administrative Security and the Prosecutor General's Corps of Technical Investigators.14 * A new criminal procedure code has been in place since January 2008, resulting in shorter pre-trial waiting periods and an improved conviction rate over the previous years.15

The Prosecutor General's Office runs a witness protection program.16 The Prosecutor General's Office investigates criminal offenses. Its Human Rights Unit, in 13 satellite offices, specialized in investigating human rights crimes. As of December 2008, more specialized prosecutors were handling an increased number of cases.17 There were incidents in the past and in 2008 when elements of the security forces acted in violation of state policy, the law and/or rules of engagement. To correct this situation, many procedures are now in place providing recourse to the rule of law for victims, for example: a. The Ministry of Defence investigated personnel suspected of collaboration with new right-wing paramilitary groups and culpable parties were handed over to civilian authorities. b. Military or civilian authorities investigated killings committed by security forces. c. Military and police accused of torture were now tried in civilian rather than military courts. d. The Ministry of Defence relieved from duty several officers and soldiers for unethical conduct.18

Furthermore, the United States Department of State Report for 200919 also states that: * Recent elections were generally considered fair and free. * The internal conflict continued between the government and terrorist organizations. * Civilian authorities generally maintained control of security forces with some exceptions. * The government has made efforts to confront human rights abuses. * The FARC and the ELN committed human rights abuses including: - Political killings; - Use of landmines; - Killing of off-duty members of security forces; - Kidnappings; - Forced displacements; - Intimidation of judges, prosecutors and witnesses; - Recruitment of child soldiers; - Attacks against human rights activists; - Killing of teachers and trade unionists; - New illegal armed groups are targets of security force action but lack the organization, search and military capacity of the former United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (AUC); * Kidnappings decreased by 18 percent. * Mass killings decreased by 13 percent. * During 2008, the Ministry of Defence relieved from duty 80 officers, 213 non-commissioned officers and several soldiers for unethical conduct.20 * Human Rights Unit obtained convictions against 421 defendants. * Eighty-seven members of Congress and other politicians were linked to paramilitary groups; some were convicted. * Paramilitary and new illegal groups operate in areas without a strong government presence. * The new judicial system has resulted in a conviction rate of 60% as opposed to the old conviction rate of 3%. * The Prosecutor General's Office operated 13 satellite offices specializing in investigating human rights crimes. * The Inspector General's Office investigates misconduct by public employees. * Government forces continue to use civilian informants. * The Government has initiated reforms to improve the human right performance of the security forces including new rules of engagement. * The Ministry of Defense reported 2,481 members of guerrilla groups demobilized. * Indigenous persons demobilized from the 34th and 6th fronts of the FARC. * The 8,000 to 9,000 member FARC and 2,000 member of ELN work together in many areas attacking government forces and demobilized paramilitary, while in other areas, they fight each other. * The FARC is reported as killing persons suspected of collaborating with government authorities (the only specific reference to Bogota is the terrorist attack on a Blockbuster outlet in January 2009). * The majority of kidnappings were reported as a result of common crimes. * The FARC and the ELN were reported as responsible for a total of 49 cases of kidnapping. * Military action freed 81 kidnap victims. * FARC and ELN established check points on rural highways. * Enhanced government security presence on major highways is reported as reducing the number of kidnappings.

This review of the United States, Department of State, Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 2009 satisfies the panel that Colombia is a functioning democracy where civilians have recourse to security forces when they require protection from criminal acts and to human rights investigators for protection from human rights abuses. Those accused of such acts are held accountable for their actions through the rule of law.

Historically, Colombians have feared left-wing guerrillas, the FARC and the National Liberation Army (ELN), and right-wing paramilitary groups such as the United Self Defence Forces of Colombia (AUC).

Many Colombian governments in the past took steps to control the FARC and the ELN with marginal success. Since 2002 the current government, with the assistance of the US, has committed significant resources to protecting its citizens from harm from the two left- wing groups.

Of particular interest in reviewing the current situation as it pertains to FARC in Colombia today, are the two reports by the International Crisis Group from April 200821 and from March 200922. Both are recent and all statements are fully documented. In addition, the Group is guided by well-known and respected international personalities, including a former Prime Minister of Canada and an internationally recognized Canadian jurist. * The first report outlines the problems that the current Uribe government has created for FARC since 2002. o Many experienced commanders have been killed by security forces, assassinated by other insurgents, or have died. This has severely disrupted communications and internal cohesion. o No Colombian political party any longer supports FARC as a legitimate left-wing force. o The FARC's command structure after six years of sustained military pressure is believed to be faltering due to a lack of internal communication. o Security forces believe that the FARC is less operational, i.e., in 2007 there were only between 9,000 to 11,000 fighters supporting FARC as opposed to approximately 19,000 in 2002 and only 10 of its former 71 fronts are currently regularly active. o The new government policy is to expand the presence of security forces in remote areas to re-establish the rule of law in these areas. o Some FARC units are trying to specialize in the use of land mines and attacks against specific police and military targets. o To compensate for losses, rural fronts are being reinforced with urban militia. o The FARC is attempting to regain legitimacy in the rural population by avoiding harm to civilians while focusing on high impact military targets. * The more recent 2009 report notes: o Key units of the FARC have withdrawn to the jungle and mountains. o New tactics rely on ambushes. o At the tactical level, structures have decentralized; however, the Secretariat is capable of coordinating actions around the country. o Even though the FARC has replaced its leaders in its senior command, coordination between senior and mid-ranking commanders is difficult. o Demobilized fighters remain in big cities to decrease the risk of being targeted by the FARC. o After pushing the FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries, the security forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. o Areas where the FARC is strong and active are noted - western Meta, Putumayo, high mountain ranges or tropical jungle. (None of these include large urban areas.) o Security forces fear the FARC will attempt to win back status in urban areas through terrorism. Police have seized caches of explosives in the outskirts and FARC commandos have been arrested when attempting to penetrate cities. The first two complete paragraphs of page 12 indicate FARC urban structures have been disrupted; however, insurgents remain active in Cali and Buenaventura. Now the FARC work in independent cells, while support networks have been progressively weakened. In the early 2000's, urban fronts were driven out of cities like Bogota, Medellin, Cali and Cucuta. Security forces have succeeded in making guerrilla logistics vulnerable to interception and now exert tight control via checkpoints on roads and rivers that lead to and from combat areas. o Extortion may have increased but is under-reported. Common criminals appear to be using the FARC's name as a means to extract extortion. o Drug revenues have dropped from one billion dollars to $500-600 million per year. o The ELN leadership has called for an alliance with the FARC; however, this generally has not occurred. In areas where ELN formations have been decimated, there have been links with FARC fronts. o Section 8 (page 15) states that, in urban areas, FARC support has vanished. Tens of thousands marched in Bogota against the FARC in March 2008. FARC continues to control remote areas. o The FARC is actively working with youth in universities to again create a base of political support. o Security forces have increased to more than 400,000 in 2007 and have been successful in forcing the FARC to retreat. Since 2007, security forces have expanded their presence in rural areas. o The insurgents are not close to defeat for a number of reasons; however, the government strategy aimed at a military victory showed visible results as of 2007. * The theme of the International Crisis Group reports is reflected in the research of the Board. Item 4.3, page 3 23 indicates that a news report in February 2008 reported that the FARC is relying more on drug trafficking for its financial support since kidnapping and extortion are in decline.
In addition, the Colombian Minister of Defence indicated to the BBC that the FARC currently does not have the communication network it used to have.

The report indicates that the FARC and the ELN engage in human rights abuses, including political killings, murder of security force personnel, kidnappings, intimidation of judges, recruitment of child soldiers and killings of teachers and trade unionists.
The report provides specifics as to murders and abductions by the FARC.

The only 2008 reference to an incident in a large urban centre occurred in September when a car bomb killed four civilians in front of a court house in Cali. This type of incident would not generally be considered a targeted killing. Many killings of former paramilitary members were reported as well as members of security forces.

This review of facts satisfies me that the State of Colombia is making serious efforts to provide adequate protection for its citizens who fear the FARC. These efforts are not always perfect but are most successful in urban areas such as Bogota. The panel is not persuaded that the claimant has met his burden of proving otherwise.

Therefore, the panel finds that another part of the city of Bogota would be a reasonable place for the claimant to settle in, considering his work background24 and the fact he has lived and survived in the U.S.A. for at least 10 years. Furthermore, the panel notes that the metropolitan area as a whole has a large population of over 8 million and has reasonable security and social services capable of meeting the needs of its inhabitants. The panel therefore, also finds that another part of Bogota would meet both requirements of a viable Internal Flight Alternative for him.

Consequently, based on the totality of the evidence adduced, including Counsel's submissions, the panel is not persuaded to believe that the claimant has a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground, or would be subjected personally to a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, should he be returned to Colombia today.

The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, determines that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX is neither a Convention refugee within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor a person in need of protection under subsection 97(1). His claim is, therefore, rejected. (signed) "W. Lim" W.
